opening.headline: What lists and settings can control employees' ability to freely connect external apps to AI?
body: Employees begin to connect their mail, document storage, messenger, and personal tools to AI. Although connectivity is convenient, data from connected apps may be transferred to and from AI. If you do not set a list of how much you will allow, it will be left to your personal judgment.

In this lesson, we'll cover the difference between whitelists and denylists, how to prevent bypass through personal accounts with validation domain restrictions, plug-ins and apps, and read and write permission scopes. Lastly, we will explain the order in which new connector requests are reviewed and how to operate after approval.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain connector whitelists and domain restrictions
You can distinguish between connectors to allow and connectors to restrict.

screens.title: Control which external apps can connect
screens.lead: Read the situations below and consider what happens when you leave the connection to your own discretion.

visual.alt: Illustration of several lines extending from the AI assistant icon to mail, document storage, messenger, and personal tools.

paragraphs: Employees are starting to connect their mail, document storage, messenger, and personal tools to AI. Once connected, AI will read your documents and summarize your messages, making your work easier. However, it also means that data from connected apps can be transferred to and from AI.
The Claude Code documentation basically tells us that anyone can connect to any MCP server they want. If no settings are made, it is up to each employee to decide whether to connect or not.
If you don't set a list of what you will allow, each person will have different standards. This class covers how to create and stick to that list.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which is safer: blocking unlisted connectors by default or blocking only known risks? Check it out in the demo.

screens.outro: First, let's think about our organization's connectivity status.

screens.title: Is there a list of allowed connectors?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. The answer will not be submitted, so think of it yourself first.

items.prompt: Is there a list of apps in my organization that can connect to AI?
items.answer: If there is no list, individual employees decide whether to connect. First, you should start by identifying which apps are currently connected.

items.prompt: Can I prevent work apps from linking to my personal account?
items.answer: Connecting your work email to AI in your personal account rather than your work account takes your company information out of your organization's control. Claude Enterprise has a setting that prevents this, and we see it in the demo.

items.prompt: When a new connector request comes in, who reviews it and based on what criteria?
items.answer: Without a person in charge and standards, each request will have a different answer. The commentary organizes the review criteria in the following order: purpose, authority, data class, and controls.

screens.outro: Now let’s look at the framework for choosing the level of control.

screens.title: White List: A Framework for Choosing the Level of Control
screens.lead: Move the slider to explore the control patterns outlined in the Claude Code article from strongest to weakest. For each value, you can see what is blocked and what is allowed.

stops.body: If you leave an empty server list in managed-mcp.json, no servers will be loaded, with a few exceptions. This is the strongest control. This can be selected in environments where external connectivity is not required for business purposes.
If you specify a server in managed-mcp.json, all users will receive the same server and will not be able to add other servers. This is appropriate when the set of approved servers is clear.

By using allowedMcpServers and allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true together, users can add servers they want within the approved list, and servers not on the list will be blocked. This is the basic blocking method and is a typical form of whitelisting. Claude Code doesn't have a built-in list of servers for users to browse, so we share the approved list on internal wikis, etc.

If you only use allowedMcpServers and do not use allowManagedMcpServersOnly, the allow list will be applied but users can expand the scope in their settings. This results in less control, requiring you to manage user settings changes separately.

deniedMcpServers blocks only known risk servers and allows all others. Since new servers cannot be blocked, the level of control is low. If you don't deploy any controls, users can add anything. Anthropic says it reviews connectors in the directory for listings but does not audit or manage security.

screens.outro: In principle, an allow list with the default block is more secure than a deny list with the default allow. Next, we will see how to prevent personal account bypass.

screens.title: Verification domain restrictions: prevent personal account bypass
screens.lead: Tap the toggle to compare how the same employee's behavior changes with Verification Domain Restrictions turned off and on.

states.label: Setting Off
states.body: Let's say an employee has two accounts: a Claude account created with his personal email and a work account created with his work email. Your corporate email domain is a domain verified by your Enterprise organization. If the setting is off, these employees can log in with their personal accounts and connect their work Gmail. This leaves company information outside of the organization's control. No matter how strict the whitelist is, it does not apply to personal accounts, so you must block this path separately.

states.label: Setting on
states.body: If you turn on the Restrict verified-domain connectors to your enterprise setting in Claude Enterprise, only accounts within your Enterprise organization can connect support connectors to email addresses in verified domains. Targets include Gmail, Google Drive, Slack, Notion, Microsoft 365, Atlassian, and more. Attempts to connect your work Gmail from your personal account will be blocked, but you will still be able to connect from your work account. However, if the linking service does not share your account identity, it cannot be verified and the connection continues as is. To set it up, your organization must have at least one verified domain.

screens.outro: Now let's expand our control to include plugins, apps, and permissions.

screens.title: Custom connectors and permission sets
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how OpenAI and Google Workspace divide and control plugins, apps, and permission scopes.

tabs.label: OpenAI plugin
tabs.body: OpenAI places separate controls on plug-in installation and access to apps within it. Select the plugin installation settings from Installable, Installable in Workspace, Customized to Role, or Inactive. The two controls are evaluated separately and may prevent you from using included apps even if the plugin is installed. New Enterprise and Edu workspaces start with only select apps turned on, and new plugins and apps are largely inactive. For Business, the app is turned on by default.

tabs.label: OpenAI app permissions
tabs.body: OpenAI divides app access and app permissions. App access determines who can use the app, and app permissions determine when the user is asked before using the app. There is also an actions item to review actions that require approval. Turning off an app will block app-based features, but may leave behind plugins or skills that don't require an app.

tabs.label: Google Workspace
tabs.body: Google Workspace controls Gemini features by turning them on and off on a per-service basis. Since reading and writing are determined by the scope of permissions granted by the connected app, first check whether a read-only connection is possible. It is consistent with the principle of least privilege to request that a connection with a wide range of privileges be narrowed to the necessary range.

tabs.label: Compare
tabs.body: All three products separately control who uses them, what is installed, and with what authority they are connected. Therefore, the whitelist must include not only names but also scope and approval conditions. Even for apps with the same name, read-only connections and write-only connections have different risks.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the governance framework, let's move on to the example of reviewing a new connector request.

screens.title: Commentary: Review criteria for new connector requests
screens.lead: The marketing team asked if they wanted to connect an external project management app to AI. Select the next arrow to walk through the four-step review.

steps.title: Step 1: Write down the purpose of your connection
steps.body: Write down what data is exchanged for which tasks. The subsequent decision depends on whether the marketing team wants AI to summarize the campaign schedule or modify task status. If the purpose is ambiguous, the request will be rejected and re-received.

steps.title: Step 2: Check permission scope
steps.body: Check whether you need read only or write as well and choose the least privilege. If your goal is to summarize your schedule, a read-only connection is sufficient. If write permission is required, write down separately what operation it is needed for.

steps.title: Step 3: View the data rating
steps.body: Verify that the level of data being linked does not exceed the acceptable product criteria. If your project management app contains personal customer information, check again to see if the products and plans are allowed in that tier.

steps.title: Step 4: Determine controls
steps.body: Decide whether to whitelist, open only to specific roles, or deny. If only the marketing team needs it, open it by role or group and do not allow transcription. We will record your decision and reasons for your request.

screens.outro: We will continue to look at the operation after permission and how to reconsider.

screens.title: Commentary: Post-permission operation and review
screens.lead: Below are the operating rules after acceptance. Select a highlighted passage to see the why and how of that rule.

data.text: Approved connectors are recorded in the allowed list together with Name, scope, approver, date. If a plugin and an app are bundled, Check app access settings separately is checked. MCP usage is reviewed to check Is a server not on the list being used?. The list is regularly re-evaluated and Unused items will be canceled.

marks.note: If you just write down your name, you won't know by what authority you approved it. The scope, approver, and date must be included so that when reviewing, the judgment at the time of approval can be confirmed.
Installing a plugin and using an app within it are separate controls. Even if you allow the plugin, you need to check separately whether app access is open.

marks.span: Is a server not on the list being used?
marks.note: Even if you create a whitelist, servers outside the list may be used due to a soft whitelist or missing settings. Compare actual and approved status with usage.
If a connection once accepted remains unused, it poses a risk. During regular review, items with no history of use are removed.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at the operating rules, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Connectors are whitelisted by default
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class.

paragraphs: The basis for connector governance is a list that allows only approved connections. Deny lists that only block known risks have less control because they do not block new servers. Listing in the directory does not imply any security audit or management.

Verification domain restrictions prevent circumvention through personal accounts. This setting limits connections to external services using company email to accounts within the organization. However, there is a limitation in that it cannot be verified unless the linking service shares the account identity.

The scope of permission is divided into read and write and is granted to a minimum. Plugin installation and app access are separate controls, so check both. New requests are reviewed in the order of purpose, permissions, data level, and controls.

Even after you allow it, the work is not over. Record the name, scope, approver, and date, check usage status, and cancel unused items. Following these three operating rules will ensure that your list remains reflective of reality over time. Your list is not a document that recorded what it was like on the day it was created; it is a document that should reflect the state of your connections today. Set a review cycle in advance, such as quarterly, and check again on the same basis when there are new connector requests or configuration changes.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The default for the list is Basic Block. Open only the approved ones and keep the rest closed.

checks.intro: See for yourself the differences in control methods. This confirmation is not logged.
checks.q: What are the characteristics of using only the denied list (deniedMcpServers) in MCP server control?
options: The strictest rule is that all servers not on the list are blocked.
Directory listing servers have been security audited so no additional controls are required
The level of control is low as only known risk servers are blocked and the rest are allowed.
It has the same effect as a whitelist, so it is equally safe.
checks.explain: The deny list is the default allow method, so it does not block unknown risky servers. The default block, whitelist, is safer.

wrong.0: The side that blocks servers that are not on the list is the whitelist.
wrong.1: Directory listing is a review basis only and does not constitute a security audit or management.
wrong.3: Default Allow and Default Block have opposite effects.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The deny list is allowed by default and does not prevent new risky servers.
checks.incorrectFeedback: You may have understood the direction of the reject list in the opposite direction. Look again at how unlisted servers are treated.

checks.intro: Consider the order in which you review new connector requests. Arrange the items in the appropriate order.
checks.q: Put new connector requests in the right order for review
items: Write down the purpose of the connection and the data being transferred.
Check the read/write permission range and select the minimum permission.
Check whether the data level to be connected does not exceed the acceptable standard.
Decide on control measures: allow list, open specific roles, or deny
checks.explain: By reviewing the order of purpose, permissions, data level, and controls, you can ensure consistent application of least privilege and rubrics.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. It is a flow that starts from the purpose and ends with control measures.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Think about what you need to know before deciding on controls.

glossary.def: This is a list of ways to allow only external apps and servers approved by your organization to connect.
An email domain that your organization has certified ownership of. This serves as the basis for domain-based restrictions.
A connection that a user adds directly from outside the directory. MCP servers are one example.
This is the distinction between whether the connected app only retrieves data or also changes it.

misconceptions.myth: Connectors listed in the directory are safe.
misconceptions.fact: This is only a review based on listing criteria and is not a security audit or management.
It blocks only known ones, so new servers remain open. A list that only allows approved items is safer.

misconceptions.myth: If you turn off the connector, the plug-in also disappears.
misconceptions.fact: Only app-based features may be blocked, leaving behind plugins or skills that don't require an app.

closing.lead: We recapitulate the key points of this lesson.
points: Prevent personal account bypass with verification domain restrictions.
Permissions are limited to read and write.
New requests are reviewed on a phased basis.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Who approves the list of external apps connected to AI in my organization, and how do I find out if a connection is made that isn't on the list?
